Architecture · Engram
Engram: look facts up instead of computing them
196B params in FP8 tables, ~16M rows per head
Known ahead: rows depend only on token IDs
So it lives in host RAM and is prefetched
Our v6e-16: 200.5 GB, 160.8 µs per step

Part 2
Kernel optimizations on TPU v6e-16
Start with the profiler: what XProf showed inside one decode step.
Kernel optimizations · motivation
XProf: where a 61.71 ms decode step went
1 · Routed MoE 20.17 ms
2 · Collectives 16.08 ms
3 4.24
Attention, dense, mHC 21.22 ms
1 · 4-bit experts ran slowly
256-row tile, only a few rows of real tokens
12 vector ops per FP4 weight block
v6e has no FP4 matmul, so every weight was unpacked by hand, and tiles were mostly padding.
2 · The network time was waiting
fast chip
slowest chip
Routing gave some chips 2.4× more work. 90.6% of the reduce was waiting; the wire (green) took 30 µs.
3 · Every KV update copied 70 MB
tile (4, 128)
flat (-1, 512)
Flattening broke TPU's memory tiling, so XLA rewrote the whole cache before and after each update.
XProf on TPU v6e-16, decode step at C = 64, 1k/1k, 16K context. Source: kernel-optimizations-recipe TECH-NOTE

Part 3
Megakernels on TPU v7x
One kernel per token: the idea, then how we built it for DeepSeek.
Megakernels · the idea
The megakernel idea: never leave the kernel
One launch per token
Next layer's weights load during this one
Collectives run inside the kernel
After Inferact, "700 TPS on Kimi K3: A Case for TPU Megakernels" (inferact.ai/blog/tpu-megakernels)
Megakernels · DeepSeek on TPU
Inside one layer of the megakernel
VMEM · one pallas_call · @pl.loop over 40 layers
1 · mHC mix 4 streams, Sinkhorn ×20 in registers
2 · Layer mode Full, Reindex or Reuse decides what to compute
3 · Sparse attention 128 window + top-512, KV resident in VMEM
4 · All-reduce remote DMA over ICI, no host
5 · Shared expert FP8, runs first and is all-reduced
6 · Router x × gate weights → 384 scores, √softplus + bias
7 · Top-6 six argmax passes, weights normalized × 1.5
8 · Expert loop lowest pending expert: DMA its FP4 weights once, apply to every row that chose it
HBM · 384 experts × 40 layers, MXFP4
only picked
VMEM 671.55 → 23.31 MiB on 16× v7 (38.20 MiB on 4× v7) by reusing buffers across layers and aliasing gate/up weights
Steps 5–8: routed megakernel, DSV4-Flash-Deployment megakernel-recipe decode_megakernel.py:1194. The timed PR #3 v7x kernel is a structural proxy: fixed expert pattern, simplified attention and mHC, no prefetch

Takeaways
1
The model saves memory by letting layers share their KV.
2
Engrams are here to stay!
3
For small number of users, running the whole model as one kernel is fastest.
Thank you!
